headline: Creates federal rules for payment stablecoins, limiting who can issue them and requiring full one-to-one backing with cash or similar safe assets.
what_it_does: Only approved issuers, such as bank subsidiaries or federally or state-approved companies, may issue payment stablecoins, which are digital coins meant to be redeemable for a fixed dollar value. Issuers must hold reserves equal to every coin they issue in cash, bank deposits, short-term Treasuries, or similar assets, publish their reserves monthly, and explain how people can cash out. Knowingly issuing without approval can bring fines of up to $1 million per violation and up to 5 years in prison. Approved stablecoins are not treated as securities or commodities, but issuers must follow anti-money laundering laws.

who_it_affects.how: They must get federal or state approval, keep one-to-one reserves, publish monthly reserve reports checked by an accounting firm, and follow capital, risk, and anti-money laundering rules.

who_it_affects.group: People who hold or use stablecoins
who_it_affects.how: Coins from approved issuers must be backed by reserves and redeemable under published policies and fees, and the law sets how holders are treated if an issuer goes bankrupt.

who_it_affects.group: Crypto exchanges and other digital asset service providers
who_it_affects.how: Three years after enactment, they may not offer or sell stablecoins in the U.S. unless the coins come from approved issuers or qualifying foreign issuers.

They can offer coins in the U.S. only if Treasury finds their home country's rules comparable, they register with the OCC, hold enough reserves in a U.S. institution in most cases, and their country is not under U.S. sanctions.

who_it_affects.group: Public companies outside the financial industry
who_it_affects.how: They may not issue payment stablecoins unless a federal review committee approves them unanimously.

who_it_affects.group: Banks, credit unions, and trust companies
who_it_affects.how: They may issue stablecoins through subsidiaries, and they keep their power to issue digital assets that represent deposits.
They must report holdings of approved stablecoins worth more than $5,000 on their financial disclosure forms.

when_it_takes_effect: The earlier of 18 months after enactment (January 18, 2027) or 120 days after regulators issue final rules; the ban on exchanges selling unapproved stablecoins starts 3 years after enactment (July 18, 2028).
